lesson.title: Calculate across the right axis

lead.text: Start with the request that touches every cell. The sheet is held by tickets = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]). Adding 2 with tickets + 2 gives [[3, 4, 5], [6, 7, 8]]. The single 2 has no grid of its own, so NumPy stretches it to fit the grid and then adds position by position. This stretching is called broadcasting. Multiplying with tickets * 10 works the same way and gives [[10, 20, 30], [40, 50, 60]].

Two arrays of the same shape combine position by position, with no stretching needed. If prices = np.array([5, 7, 9]) and sold = np.array([2, 1, 3]), then prices * sold is [10, 7, 27], which is 5 × 2, 7 × 1 and 9 × 3. Each product comes from matching positions, so the result has the shape of the inputs. In neither case does the code contain a loop.
Decide whether the single number is added once or reaches every element.
The 2 reaches every element before you add the elements up.

The second request goes the other way. Instead of changing every cell, it asks for one number that summarises many. tickets.sum() adds all six values and gives 21. tickets.mean() adds them and divides by how many there are, giving 3.5. Methods like these are called reductions, because they reduce many values to one.

A single total for the whole sheet is rarely what the manager wants. She wants the total for each day and the total for each showing. Those need the grid divided up in a chosen way, and NumPy has to be told which way. That choice is the next idea.

Each direction through the grid is an axis. Axis 0 runs down, from one row to the next. Axis 1 runs across, from one column to the next. The axis you name is the one that gets combined. sum(axis=0) adds down each column and leaves one total per column. sum(axis=1) adds across each row and leaves one total per row. Step through both on the sheet.

afterFigure.text: On the sheet, axis=0 gives [5, 7, 9]. The middle showing sold 7 tickets over the two days, which answers the manager's first request. axis=1 gives [6, 15], the total for each day. The result always has one axis fewer than the grid, so a grid with two axes becomes a single line. mean takes the axis in the same way, so mean(axis=1) gives the average for each row.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
result = a.sum(axis=0)

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
result = a.sum(axis=1)

lead.text: Decide which axis leaves one total for each column.

steps.headline: What does sum(axis=1) give for np.array([[3, 1], [2, 5]])?

lead.text: Add across each row of a small grid.

workedSteps.text: axis=1 adds across each row. The first row holds 3 and 1.

steps.headline: For np.array([[2, 4], [6, 8]]), what does sum(axis=0) give?

workedSteps.text: axis=0 adds down each column. The first column holds 2 and 6. What is its total?
The second column holds 4 and 8. What is its total?

steps.headline: A row added to every row

lead.text: Broadcasting also works between a grid and a shorter array. Suppose a different amount has to be added to each showing: 10 more tickets for the first and 20 for the second. A line of two numbers, np.array([10, 20]), can be added to a grid with two columns. NumPy lines the short array up with the last dimension and repeats it down the rows, so every row gets the same two additions. The short array's length has to match the number of columns. Step through the picture, where the same grid also gets a single 10.

afterFigure.text: In the first case each row receives 10 in its first column and 20 in its second, giving [[11, 22], [13, 24]]. In the second case the single 10 reaches every cell. When the lengths cannot be lined up this way, such as an array of three numbers against two columns, NumPy stops with an error.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
result = a + np.array([10, 20])

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
result = a + 10

lead.text: The short array is repeated for every row. Work out the four results, then add them.

The last request was a copy of the sheet, and it raises a question about slices. Slicing an array with a[:2] gives a view, a window onto the same stored numbers and not a new set. A view takes almost no extra memory, which suits large data. It also has a consequence: changing the view changes the original, because the two share one set of numbers. In the picture, b = a[:2] followed by b[0] = 99 changes a[0] as well.

When you want numbers that can be changed freely, ask for a copy with the copy method. a[:2].copy() makes independent storage, and edits to it leave a alone. A list slice behaves differently, since it always builds a new list, so the habit from lists needs adjusting. Step through both cases.

afterFigure.text: With the view, b[0] = 99 shows up in a as well: a becomes [99, 4, 6]. With the copy, a stays [2, 4, 6] and only b changes. When an array has to stay as it was, copy before editing.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([2, 4, 6])
b = a[:2]
b[0] = 99

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([2, 4, 6])
b = a[:2].copy()
b[0] = 99

lead.text: Decide whether the changed array shares its numbers with a.

lesson.orientation: Apply elementwise operations, broadcasting and reductions.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: A booking sheet for a small hall has two rows of numbers. Row one reads 1, 2, 3 and row two reads 4, 5, 6, standing for tickets sold at three showings on each of two days. The manager has three requests. She wants the tickets sold at the middle showing over the two days, the total for each day, and a copy of the sheet with every figure raised by two.

On paper each request is easy, and each one asks for a different movement across the grid. The middle showing needs one number from each row. Each day's total needs the numbers within a row. The rise applies to every cell. The arrays from the last lesson can answer all three in a line each, provided the direction of the calculation is clear.

This lesson works through those requests on the small sheet. It begins with changing every value at once and moves on to adding up in a chosen direction. It ends with a warning about what happens when you edit a piece of an array.

intro.promise: By the end you'll predict an array calculation, choose which axis to combine along, and know when editing a slice changes the original.

recap.keyIdea: Array arithmetic applies to every element, axis=0 combines down columns and axis=1 across rows, and a basic slice is a view unless you copy it.

blocks.text: You found that the middle showing sold 7 tickets over the two days, by adding down a column. You also found that np.array([1, 3, 5]) + 2 sums to 15, and that editing a copy left the original's first value at 7.

recap.nextHook: Every array in this lesson was typed out by hand. Real data usually has a pattern: readings at regular distances along a path, or random draws that have to be repeatable. The next lesson shows how arange and linspace lay values out between two ends, and how a seeded generator makes random numbers that can be reproduced.

questions.prompt: What is the sum of np.array([1, 3, 5]) + 2?
hints: Add the scalar to every element.
Broadcast the addition to every position.
questions.onCorrect: 15. The 2 reached every element, giving 3, 5 and 7, which sum to 15.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the 2 once to the total. It is added to each element.

questions.prompt: For [[2, 4], [6, 8]], what is the first value of sum(axis=0)?
hints: axis=0 combines the rows at each column.
The first column holds the values in the first position of each row.
Add the top-left and bottom-left values.
questions.onCorrect: 8. The first column holds 2 and 6, and axis=0 added down it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sum of the first row. axis=0 adds down a column and not across a row.
That is the second column's total. The question asks for the first.

questions.prompt: With a = np.array([[5, 6], [7, 8]]) and b = np.array([1, 2]), what is the sum of all values in a + b?
hints: b is combined with every row of a.
The first column gets 1 added, the second gets 2.
Add the four results.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: a + b is [[6, 8], [8, 10]], whose sum is 32.

questions.onCorrect: 32. Every row got the offsets 1 and 2 added, giving 6, 8, 8 and 10.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total of a alone. b adds to every row.
That adds b only once. It is combined with each row.

questions.prompt: With a = np.array([7, 8, 9]), b = a[:2].copy() and b[0] = 50, what is a[0]?
hints: Does the copy share data with a?
copy makes independent storage.
Which value did a start with in its first position?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The copy is independent, so a[0] is still 7.

questions.onCorrect: 7. The copy owns its own data, so changing b left a alone.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what a view would show. The copy method separated the data.

questions.prompt: For [[3, 7], [2, 8]], what is the second value of mean(axis=1)?
hints: Reduce the columns within the second row.
axis=1 reduces each row separately.
Add the second row and divide by its length.
questions.onCorrect: 5. The second row holds 2 and 8, and their mean is 5.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the second value of the first row. The second row holds 2 and 8.
That is the second row's sum. The mean divides it by the length.

hints: A basic slice shares the original data.
b points into the storage of a.
The write to b[1] changes the same element as a[1].

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: b is a view into a, so the write changes a[1] to 20.

questions.onCorrect: 20. b is a view into a, so the write changed a's element.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the value before the write. The slice shares a's data, so the write shows.

hints: Equal shapes multiply position by position.
Match 2 with 1, 4 with 2 and 8 with 3.
Add the three products.
questions.prompt: What is the sum of np.array([2, 4, 8]) * np.array([1, 2, 3])?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The products are 2, 8 and 24. They sum to 34.

questions.onCorrect: 34. The products are 2, 8 and 24, formed position by position.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds up the first array alone. Multiply matching positions, then add.
That multiplies the sums. Multiply matching positions instead.

hints: Which number is in the middle of each row?
The middle column holds one number from each row.
Add those two numbers.
questions.prompt: What do the middle numbers of the two rows add up to?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The middle column holds 2 and 5, and 2 + 5 = 7.

questions.onCorrect: 7. You added down the middle column. That is a total taken along one direction of a grid, which NumPy calls an axis.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds every number in the second row... check that you used one number from each row.
That is only the middle of the first row... you need both rows.

hints: Is the 10 added once or to each element?

choices.label: An error, because the shapes differ

questions.onCorrect: An array holding 11 and 12. The single value was stretched across the array and added to each element.

misconceptions.feedback: That would append 10. + on arrays adds to every element.
A single value always broadcasts. No error occurs.

hints: Which axis runs down the rows, combining them?
questions.prompt: Which call gives one total per column?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: axis=0 combines the rows, leaving one total per column.

questions.onCorrect: sum(axis=0). It adds down each column, leaving one total per column.

misconceptions.feedback: axis=1 adds across each row, leaving one total per row.
A two-dimensional array has only axes 0 and 1.

hints: What does axis=1 leave behind: a total per row or per column?
questions.prompt: Why does the result hold two numbers?

choices.label: There are two rows, and axis=1 gives one total per row
There are two columns, and axis=1 keeps both

acceptedIdeas: There are two rows, and axis=1 gives one total per row
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: axis=1 leaves one total per row, and there are two rows.

questions.onCorrect: There are two rows, and axis=1 gives one total per row.

misconceptions.feedback: The columns were added together. Each row became one number.
The count of results depends on the array. Here there were two rows.

hints: Which values sit in the second position of each row?
They are 4 and 8.
Add the two values.
questions.prompt: What is the total of the second column?
questions.onCorrect: 12. The second column holds 4 and 8, so sum(axis=0) gives 12 for it.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 6 and 8, the second row. A column takes one value from each row.
